sections.body:
An argument has a claim, a reason, and a criterion that says when the claim has been met. In a clean argument the claim stays in the same place. The ground does not move. A manipulated argument is one in which the ground moves: the talk leaves the claim and turns to the person, to the feeling, to the title of the speaker, or to a standard that is brought in after the facts have arrived. Every fact can be true and the argument still lost, because nothing was ever tested against anything.

Two things usually happen together. First, the person replaces the claim: the question becomes whether the speaker is competent, honest or likeable, and the original question is never answered. Second, the criterion moves: the standard used to judge the claim is raised, lowered or replaced once the other side has produced its evidence. The speaker has not shown the claim to be wrong. The speaker has changed the place where the claim was going to be measured.

This article uses the word **fallacy** for these moves. A fallacy is an error in the shape of an argument — a move that breaks the reasoning instead of answering the claim. It is not an insult and not a diagnosis. Strong feeling, a bad memory, a wrong fact and a genuine disagreement are not fallacies. A person can make a fallacy in a good mood and mean it honestly. A person can also argue correctly and be unpleasant; the argument can be sound while the manner is not. Naming the move tells you where the exchange is going. It does not tell you what the other person is.

The cost of a manipulated argument is not the sentence. It is the delay. The answer that was ready never gets asked, the decision is made on the ground that has been moved, and nobody can say afterwards which part of the claim was ever in dispute. Once you can name the move, you can answer it in one sentence, put the ground back, and keep the argument about the claim.
examples: The facts were not in dispute; only the ground under them was.
The question stopped being about the schedule and became about the person who wrote it.
A fallacy describes the move, not the person.
sections.heading: When an argument stops being about the claim

terms.example: It was manipulation: the question about the schedule became a question about the person.
terms.gloss: The arranging of an exchange so that the ground under the claim moves and the claim is never tested.

terms.example: Calling the move a fallacy describes it; it does not insult the person.
terms.gloss: An error in the shape of an argument, a move that breaks the reasoning instead of answering the claim.

sections.body:
Five moves carry most of the weight, and you will recognise them by their words before you remember their names. The first is the either-or that is not an either-or. A **false dilemma** offers two options and pretends that no third option exists: *"Either we cut the budget by a third, or the service stops."* Often a third option exists and nobody says it out loud: a smaller cut, a delay, a different month, a cheaper supplier. The tell is not the number of options but whether the speaker had to mention the third one. Ask what else was considered; if the answer is *"there is no other way"*, ask who checked.

The second move hides its conclusion inside a question. A **loaded question** carries the answer in its own wording, so that any reply confirms it. *"When will you stop making excuses?"* assumes two things: that there are excuses, and that there is a reason to stop. The words to listen for are the ones that smuggle in a verdict — *always*, *never*, *still*, *obviously*. The way to put the ground back is to answer the question that was actually asked: *"Which part of the plan do you want to check?"*

The third move happens after the facts have arrived. **Goalpost shifting** is the moving of the criterion once the other side has met it: the requirement was *"at least three independent sources"*, and when three sources arrive the requirement is *"and all of them in writing, from outside the company"*. Nothing has been proved wrong, because nothing was tested against the standard that was in force when the claim was made. The short answer is to fix the criterion before the answer: *"Let us agree now on what would count as an answer, so we are both using the same one."*

Two more moves change who decides. An **appeal to emotion** replaces the reason with a feeling: *"After everything I have done for this team, you want me to give it up?"* The feeling may be real, and the answer may still deserve to be tested. An **appeal to authority** replaces the reason with a title: *"The chief engineer says this design is safe, so we do not need the test."* An expert opinion is a good reason when the expert knows this case and shows the evidence. It stops being one when the title is offered in place of the evidence. The same move appears with a crowd in it: *"Nobody else questions this."* The fact that other people do something tells you about other people, not about this claim.
examples: What else did we consider? Let us write the other options down.
Which part of the plan do you want to check?
Let us agree now on what would count as an answer.
What did they check, and can we see it?
sections.heading: The moves you will actually hear

terms.example: Either we cut the budget by a third, or the service stops — that is a false dilemma.
terms.gloss: The presenting of two options as if no other option existed.

terms.example: When will you stop making excuses? is a loaded question.
terms.gloss: A question that carries its own answer inside its wording.

terms.example: Three sources were required, then written external sources were required: that was goalpost shifting.
terms.gloss: The moving of the criterion after the other side has met it.

terms.example: After everything I have done for this team was an appeal to emotion, not a reason.
terms.gloss: The replacing of a reason with a feeling, and the treatment of the feeling as the answer.

terms.example: The chief engineer says it is safe was an appeal to authority, because no evidence was shown.
terms.gloss: The replacing of a reason with the title or the status of the person who offers it.

sections.body:
These are the words used in arguments, in training, in mediation and in the reports written after a meeting has gone wrong. They are worth learning for one reason: a name you can use is a move you can see. The first six are already on the table — **fallacy**, **false dilemma**, **loaded question**, **goalpost shifting**, **appeal to emotion** and **appeal to authority**. The rest of the vocabulary names the moves that turn the argument away from the claim altogether.

A **straw man** is an argument that nobody made. Your opponent says *"the schedule is too short for the migration"*, and the reply is *"so you want to abandon the project"*. The reply attacks a position that was never stated, and it is easy to win, because the position it attacks is weak. An **ad hominem** is the attack on the person instead of the claim: *"you did not read the last report, so your opinion does not count"*. The person may be wrong, careless or unhelpful. None of that makes the claim true or false. The claim still has to be tested.

Two words are often used for the same move. **Whataboutism** turns the answer into an answer about somebody else: *"you did it last year"*, *"what about the other team?"*. The formal name for it is **tu quoque**, which is Latin for *"you too"*. It works by making the other side's record as bad as yours, so that nobody has to answer the question. A **sunk cost** is money, time or effort that has already been spent, used as the reason to continue: *"we have paid for the training, so we might as well finish"*. What is already spent cannot be brought back by spending more. The only question left is what to do now.

The last two words are the ones on your own side of the exchange, and they are the ones you can use well. **Framing** is the way a claim is presented before it is argued. The same fact in a different frame lands differently: *"the programme cut waiting times by a third"* and *"the programme removed a third of the service"* are about one fact, and the frame decides what the reader feels before a single reason is given. **Rebuttal** is the answer itself: a reply that takes the point that was made and answers it with a reason. A rebuttal names the claim, gives the reason, and asks for the same test on the other side. Naming a fallacy is not a rebuttal. It says *"the move is wrong"*. A rebuttal says *"here is why the claim does not follow"*.
examples: That reply attacked an argument nobody made, so it answered nothing.
The question is the schedule, not your record of last year.
The same fact, put in a different frame, asks for a different decision.
A rebuttal gives the reason; naming the move only gives the label.
sections.heading: The words of the subject

terms.example: So you want to drop the whole project was a straw man; the speaker had only said the schedule was short.
terms.gloss: An argument that nobody made, set up so that it can be knocked down easily.

terms.example: You did not read the report, so your opinion does not count is an ad hominem.
terms.gloss: An attack on the person instead of on the claim.

terms.example: You did the same thing last year is whataboutism: it answers nothing.
terms.gloss: The turning of an answer into an answer about somebody else.

terms.example: The reply was a tu quoque: it pointed at the other person's record and stayed there.
terms.gloss: The formal name for whataboutism; it means "you too".

terms.example: We have paid for the training, so we might as well finish is an argument from sunk cost.
terms.gloss: Money, time or effort that has already been spent, used as the reason to spend more.

terms.example: Waiting times fell by a third and a third of the service was removed are two frames of one fact.
terms.gloss: The way a claim is presented before it is argued, which decides how the reader receives it.

terms.example: The rebuttal gave the reason and asked for the same test on the other side.
terms.gloss: A reply that takes the point that was made and answers it with a reason.

sections.body:
The nine moves below are the ones you will meet most often. Read the second column first. The words are what you will actually hear, and they are easier to recognise than the definitions.

Each move has a defect and a repair. The defect is in the third column: what the move does to the argument. The repair is in the fourth: one sentence that puts the ground back. The sentence is short on purpose. A long answer gives the other side more to work with, and the exchange leaves the claim behind.
examples: Only two left — so how many are there, and who counts them?
Please send me the terms in writing.
I want the price in an email I can read later.
sections.heading: The move, the words, what it does, and the sentence that answers it

headers: What it does to the argument
rows: False dilemma
"Either we cut the budget by a third, or the service stops."
Hides the third option, so the choice looks forced when it is not.
"What else did we consider? Let us write the other options down."
Loaded question
"When will you stop making excuses?"
Puts the conclusion in the question, so every answer confirms it.
"Which part of the plan do you want to check?"
Goalpost shifting
"Three sources are not enough. We need written sources, and all of them external."
Moves the criterion after the facts arrive, so nothing can ever pass it.
"Let us fix now what counts as an answer, and use that one."
Appeal to emotion
"After everything I have done for this team, you want me to give it up?"
Replaces the reason with a feeling, and then treats the feeling as the answer.
"I hear how much this costs you. Now let us check the plan itself."
Appeal to authority
"The chief engineer says it is safe, so the test is unnecessary."
Puts the decision in the hands of a title, and stops the evidence from being asked for.
"What did they check, and can we see it?"
Straw man
"So you want to drop the whole project."
Attacks a claim nobody made, and wins against a weak version of it.
"I said the schedule is short. That is not the same as dropping the project."
Ad hominem
"You did not read the last report, so your opinion does not count."
Replaces the claim with the person, so the claim itself is never tested.
"Let us look at the report, and then at the point."
Whataboutism (tu quoque)
"You did the same thing last year. What about the other team?"
Turns the answer into an answer about somebody else, so nobody has to reply.
"That is a separate question. Here is the answer to mine."
Sunk cost
"We have paid for the training, so we might as well finish."
Uses money that is already spent as the reason to spend more.
"The training is spent. The question is what we do now."

sections.body:
Five steps. They take seconds, they need no tool, and they work in a meeting, in a message and at home. The order matters: the first step slows the exchange down, and the last one decides whether to go on at all.

Two rules run through all five. You are describing a move, not a person, and you are asking for a test rather than demanding a concession. A sentence that begins with *"you are"* is much harder to hear than a sentence that begins with *"the question is"*.
examples: Let us leave the person out of it and look at the schedule.
What would count as an answer here?
The question was when the migration can finish. That is what I am answering.
sections.heading: How to keep an argument clean
steps: Name the move once, and move on: "This is the only two options we have, and I think there is a third." Do not name it twice. The second time sounds like a score.
Ask for the criterion: "What would count as an answer here?" Write it down before the answer comes, so the standard cannot move later.
Separate the person from the claim: "Let us leave the person out of it and look at the schedule." If the person really is the problem, say so about their work, not about their character.
Put the question back: "The question was when the migration can finish. That is what I am answering." Restate the original question in your own words before you reply to the new one.
Stop when the exchange has nothing left to test: "We are repeating the same point with different words. I will leave it here." Say it once, plainly, and end the exchange.

sections.body:
This article does not turn every disagreement into a fallacy. Two people can look at the same evidence and weigh it differently, and neither of them has made a mistake. Some of the moves named here are also honest shortcuts, used by people who mean well and are in a hurry. The test is not the feeling of the exchange. It is whether the claim is still on the table and still has a standard to be measured against.

It also does not replace listening with scoring. A fallacy is a description of a move, not an insult, and it is not a diagnosis of anybody. Naming the move well takes practice, and a wrong name is worse than no name: it makes the other side defend themselves instead of answering the question. If you are not sure which move it is, describe what happened and ask the question — *"is that the only option?"*, *"what would count as an answer?"* — and the name will usually follow on its own.

And it does not make you right. Finding a fallacy in somebody else's argument tells you that their argument has a defect. It tells you nothing about yours. Check your own move with the same five steps.
examples: Two people can read the same evidence differently, and neither has made a fallacy.
A name is a description of a move, not a verdict on a person.
If you are not sure of the name, describe the move and ask the question.
Finding a flaw in their argument says nothing about mine.
sections.heading: What this article does not do

sections.body:
Use these at the moment the exchange turns, not afterwards. The first pair is for a meeting. The second is for an argument with a partner. The third is for a group chat. The last is for writing.

None of them needs a hard voice. The point is not to win the room. The point is to put the ground back where it was, so that the claim can still be tested.
examples: Before we decide, let us agree on the criterion we are both using.
That is the question about the plan. Let us keep it there.
I can see this matters to you, and I still want to check the plan itself.
I am not asking whether you are a good person. I am asking what we do about the delay.
Let me read the whole thread before I answer the screenshot.
I am answering the point, not the person who sent it.
This paragraph answers the objection, and does not repeat the insult.
For the record, the criterion is the one written in the request.
sections.heading: Sentences you can use

sections.body:
In a room, a manipulated argument is easy to interrupt. In writing, it is not. The exchange is written down, so the ground can be moved while the reader is elsewhere, and the reader cannot hear the tone. A sentence that would sound like a question on the phone becomes a statement in a message: *"so the plan is already late, as usual"*.

Written arguments have three features that spoken ones do not. They can be **copied out of context**, so a reply has to answer the sentence as it stands, not the paragraph it came from. They are **read by people who were not there**, so they carry no tone, no pause and no face to read. And they are **answered later**, often by somebody who has only the screenshot. Each of those three features makes the moves easier to use and harder to spot.

The repair in writing is to write the ground into the text: state the question first, state the criterion, answer the objection that was actually made, and quote somebody else's words exactly when you copy them. In a group chat the same rules apply, with one addition — write for the reader who is not in the room and never will be. A message that only makes sense after three replies, and an insult pasted under somebody else's sentence, are the two commonest ways a written argument becomes a distorted one. Both are fixed by the same habit: put the claim, the criterion and the answer in the message itself. And when you are the one being pushed, slow the reply down. Read the message twice, answer the claim and not the tone, and ask for the original thread before you answer half of it.
examples: Let me read the whole exchange before I reply to half of it.
I am answering the point, not the tone.
For the record, the criterion is the one written in the request.
sections.heading: The same moves in writing and online

item.summary: An argument can be lost without a single false fact. When the ground moves — to the person, to the feeling, to a standard that changes after the facts arrive — the claim is never tested. After reading this you can name the nine moves, spot them in a live exchange, answer each one with one sentence, and keep your own argument clean when you are being pushed.
item.title: Psychological Manipulation in Arguments
